title: Ashwin Slams Hope's Tactics: Hosein Spell Like Feeding Goat to Hungry Lion
excerpt: The former India spinner said persisting with Akeal Hosein for three powerplay overs let a struggling Sanju Samson find rhythm — "Samson simply took advantage of the opportunity."
body:
• Ashwin argued on his YouTube channel that bowling left-arm spinner Akeal Hosein for three straight powerplay overs against Sanju Samson was like "serving a hungry lion a goat on a platter."
  • Samson, short of runs coming in, took 35 runs off 13 balls from Hosein — including four consecutive boundaries — and finished with 82 off 41.
  • India posted 249/5, but Shai Hope's unbeaten 102 off 45 carried West Indies to the highest successful T20I chase ever (250) with nine balls to spare.
  • The five-match series is level 1-1 after the Ranchi run-fest at the JSCA International Stadium on October 9.

Former India off-spinner Ravichandran Ashwin has delivered a blistering verdict on West Indies captain Shai Hope's tactics in the second T20I against India, arguing that persisting with left-arm spinner Akeal Hosein against Sanju Samson in the powerplay was a self-inflicted wound — "like serving a hungry lion a goat on a platter."

The analysis came during a discussion on Ashwin's YouTube channel, "Ash ki Baat," after Friday's high-scoring encounter in Ranchi. India posted 249 for 5, powered by Samson's 82 off 41 balls, but West Indies completed a stunning six-wicket win in 18.3 overs — the highest successful run chase in T20 international history — with Hope himself unbeaten on 102 off 45.

The tactical call Ashwin questioned

Ashwin's critique focused on the first six overs of India's innings. Hope bowled Hosein for three consecutive overs inside the powerplay against Samson, and the opener seized the matchup: he faced 13 balls from Hosein and took 35 runs off them, including four consecutive boundaries in the fifth over. Samson reached fifty in 21 deliveries.

Ashwin's point was that Samson arrived at the crease short of form — coming off a string of low scores, including 11 in the series opener in Lucknow on October 6 — and Hope effectively handed him the perfect conditions to find rhythm. "Samson looked scratchy because he was not in a run-scoring phase," Ashwin said. "However, Shai Hope also made a mistake today. You cannot keep using spinners from one end in an attempt to build pressure on Sanju Samson. Bowling three consecutive overs from Akeal Hosein during the powerplay was like serving a hungry lion a goat on a platter. Samson simply took advantage of the opportunity and went after Akeal Hosein."

Context & Background

The mismatch logic behind Ashwin's criticism is specific to Samson's game. The Kerala wicketkeeper-batter is one of India's most destructive players of spin; bowling a left-arm spinner into him, over after over, without variation, gave him the one thing a struggling batter craves — a predictable, repeatable rhythm. Ashwin argued Hope should have rotated his bowling options rather than letting Samson settle against a single bowler.

There is a wrinkle worth noting: Hope's decision, by the narrowest of margins, did not decide the game. West Indies won anyway, chasing 250 with nine balls to spare. Hope and Sherfane Rutherford (84 off 37) put on a 120-run fourth-wicket stand that transformed the contest, and the combined 501 runs were the second-highest match aggregate in men's T20I history. Dew at the JSCA International Stadium made defending a mountain increasingly difficult — India's attack had no answer once Hope accelerated.

Impact & Analysis

Ashwin also spent part of his analysis on Samson himself, and this is where the segment became less a critique and more a portrait of intent. He argued it is not easy to keep playing high-risk cricket when your place is under threat: "It is not easy to maintain that attitude. It is human nature that when you are in danger and know that you might be dropped, self-preservation becomes the top priority. Yet, he continues to take risks for the team." He noted Samson's luck too — a catch went straight to a fielder's hands and was dropped — but credited the approach rather than the fortune.

For the series, the math is simple: level at 1-1 with three matches to play, after India's win in Lucknow and West Indies' record chase in Ranchi. For West Indies, the comeback validates a young side — Ashwin himself said the visitors "have already accomplished more on this tour than they have in many years," given the absence of experienced campaigners like Nicholas Pooran and Kieron Pollard. For Hope, the century was personal validation too: joint-fastest T20I hundred against India, Player of the Match, and a case for IPL recruitment.

Diaspora Angle

Among Indian cricket fans, Ashwin's YouTube show has become one of the most watched post-match analysis platforms — his straight-talking, ex-player breakdowns reach millions, and this "hungry lion" segment is already among his most quoted. The Samson redemption arc also resonates: a talented, long-waited wicketkeeper playing under constant selection pressure is one of the most debated topics in Indian cricket discourse at home and abroad.

What's Next

The series moves on with three T20Is remaining, and both captains have tactical homework. India's head coach Gautam Gambhir called Hope "a world-class cricketer" while defending his own flexible batting order after Shivam Dube's promotion to No. 4 yielded five off seven balls. West Indies will need to prove Ranchi was not a dew-assisted one-off; India will need to solve a West Indies middle order that now believes it can chase anything. The next match will show whether Hope adjusts his powerplay bowling plans — or doubles down.
